Monday-Tuesday: The upper-level ridge will begin to slowly 
flatten today and Tuesday as a broad upper-level crosses over 
130W and shortwaves begin ejecting into British Columbia. Bands 
of high clouds will pass through the region at times over the 
next few days but conditions will remain dry. Monday will remain
mild with temperatures within 1-2 degrees of Sunday then cool 
5-10 degrees heading into Tuesday with the arrival of a weak 
cool front. Winds for much of the region will remain light 
today. There will be a noticeable increase in afternoon and 
evening breezes across the Okanogan Valley and through the 
Cascade river valleys starting off from the south/southeast then
shifting to the west and northwest in the evening. Winds for 
Tuesday will become a bit more breezy region-wide as cooler air 
begins to bleed into the region. West to southwest winds will 
increase closer to 10-15 mph with gusts 20-25 mph and locally 
stronger through the windier Cascade gaps. 

Wednesday-weekend: A broad upper-level trough will become 
established over the Eastern Pacific and Northwest by Wednesday
with temperatures cooling further and residual breeziness. A 
reinforcing shot of cooler air and shortwave dropping into the 
offshore trough on Thursday will dig into the base of the trough
allowing flow to buckle slightly over the Inland NW. This has 
potential to warm temperatures another 1-5 degrees from 
Wednesday but largely unrealized in Central WA and most 
noticeable in far southeastern WA and the lower Idaho Panhandle 
including the L-C Valley where highs will rebound closer to 80F.

Confidence continues to increase for a more robust trough and 
cold front Friday. There remains considerable timing differences
still varying from Thursday night to Friday afternoon dialing
int the frontal passage timing. Confidence is high for 
increased winds with this system due to a 8C cooling of the air 
mass but impacts and precise speeds will heavily depend on if 
this front passes through during peak heating or overnight as
well as how quickly the system passes through. A scenario with 
a slower passage and overnight would deliver the lighter side of
the wind outcomes with gusts mainly 15-25 mph. A scenario with 
an afternoon passage and swift progression of the front would 
be a windy outcome with gusts 25-35 mph and local gusts around 
40 mph. The latest probabilities from the NBM come with a 60-80%
chance for wind gusts at least 20 mph, 20-50% for 30 mph, and 
10-15% chance for 40 mph. The windier solution would also
suggest sustained winds of 15-25 mph for our windier areas 
from the East Slopes to the Palouse. This is something we will
need to monitor closely in the coming days.

The system will also deliver cooler temperatures with highs cooling 
from the 70s Wednesday and Thursday then into the 60s Friday 
into the weekend. Some mountain valleys may be flirting with 
freezing over temperatures heading into the weekend. 

As for precipitation, ensembles are indicating a 50-60% chance for 
at least 0.10" along the Cascade Crest and mountains of NE WA 
and N ID. The potential outcomes for these areas are as high as
0.50 inches or more. This could equate to several inches of 
snow for some of the highest peaks. Confidence is much lower 
for rainfall amounts outside of these areas and will depend on
the speed of the trough Friday-Saturday. There has been an 
increase in probabilities for at least some rainfall region- 
wide and this seems logical given the strong forcing expected 
along this frontal boundary. Additional precipitation chances
could come in the post frontal air mass with convective showers
under the cool pool. Latest guidance has increased the chance
for a tenth of rain toward 20-40% for locations like Lewiston,
Pullman, Spokane, Kellogg, Colville, and Omak. Outlooks are not
as favorable in the lee of the Cascades with probabilities less
than 20% for locations like Ephrata and Moses Lake. Wenatchee
and Chelan are closer to 20%. There is a slight chance for 
isolated thunderstorms Friday with the frontal passage but this 
comes with very low confidence.

Snow levels in the Cascades will dip toward 6500 feet Friday and 
5500 feet Friday night into Saturday morning. Those venturing 
into the high country should be prepared for cooler temperatures
and wet conditions. At this time, snow accumulations look light
but a few of the highest peaks near the immediate Cascade crest
could pick up several inches. /sb
